title: Shock Absorber Replacement
summary: Shock absorber blueprint for confirming poor damping, leakage, mounting noise, and paired replacement context before quoting rear shock service.
symptoms: Bouncy ride, rear float, or poor control after bumps
Rear clunk from worn shock bushings or mounts
Fluid leakage from the shock body
Cupped tires or unstable braking and lane-change behavior
inspect_first: Shock body leakage, denting, shaft condition, and bushing/mount wear
Upper and lower mounting hardware condition and corrosion
Rear springs, control arms, sway links, and tire wear pattern
Ride height and load-related symptoms before quoting shocks alone
likely_causes: Loose rear suspension link or spring issue imitating shock noise
repair_overview: Confirm damping failure or mounting noise with visual inspection and road-test behavior.
Support the vehicle and suspension safely before removing shock hardware.
Remove upper and lower fasteners, accounting for trunk, wheel well, or underbody access.
Install shocks in pairs when appropriate, transfer hardware if required, and torque at ride height when specified.
Road test for noise and ride control, then recheck fastener and mount seating.
common_mistakes: Quoting shocks for a clunk caused by sway links, bushings, or loose hardware
Replacing only one side when paired damping balance matters
Ignoring rusted or broken upper mounts during the estimate
Tightening bushings at full droop when ride-height torque is required
estimate_guidance: Quote rear shocks as a pair when matching damping and customer expectations matter.
Flag upper mount access, rusted bolts, and broken hardware as labor variables.
Add mounts or bushings only when inspection shows wear or noise.
Mention that tires, springs, and bushings can mimic poor shock performance.
